{{Short description|Term in combinatorics}}
{{about||the set of elements in one set but not another|Relative complement|the set of differences of pairs of elements|Minkowski difference}}
In [[combinatorics]], a <math>(v,k,\lambda)</math> '''difference set''' is a subset <math>D</math> of [[cardinality|size]] <math>k</math> of a [[group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math> of [[order of a group|order]] <math>v</math> such that every non-[[identity element|identity]] element of <math>G</math> can be expressed as a product <math>d_1d_2^{-1}</math> of elements of <math>D</math> in exactly <math>\lambda</math> ways. A difference set <math>D</math> is said to be ''cyclic'', ''abelian'', ''non-abelian'', etc., if the group <math>G</math> has the corresponding property. A difference set with <math>\lambda = 1</math> is sometimes called ''planar'' or ''simple''.<ref>{{harvnb|van Lint|Wilson|1992|loc=p. 331}}</ref> If <math>G</math> is an [[abelian group]] written in additive notation, the defining condition is that every non-zero element of <math>G</math> can be written as a ''difference'' of elements of <math>D</math> in exactly <math>\lambda</math> ways. The term "difference set" arises in this way.

==Basic facts==
* A simple counting argument shows that there are exactly <math>k^2-k</math> pairs of elements from <math>D</math> that will yield nonidentity elements, so every difference set must satisfy the equation <math>k^2-k=(v-1)\lambda.</math>
* The parameter <math>n=k-\lambda</math> is called the '''order''' of the difference set.
* If <math>D</math> is a difference set and <math>g \in G,</math> then <math>gD=\{gd:d\in D\}</math> is also a difference set, and is called a '''translate''' of <math>D</math> (<math>D + g</math> in additive notation).
* The complement of a <math>(v,k,\lambda)</math>-difference set is a <math>(v,v-k,v-2k+\lambda)</math>-difference set.<ref>{{harvnb|Wallis|1988|loc=p. 61 - Theorem 4.5}}</ref>
* The set of all translates of a difference set <math>D</math> forms a [[Block design#Symmetric BIBDs|symmetric block design]], called the ''development'' of <math>D</math> and denoted by <math>dev(D).</math> In such a design there are <math>v</math> ''elements'' (usually called points) and <math>v</math> ''blocks'' (subsets). Each block of the design consists of <math>k</math> points, each point is contained in <math>k</math> blocks. Any two blocks have exactly <math>\lambda</math> elements in common and any two points are simultaneously contained in exactly <math>\lambda</math> blocks. The group <math>G</math> [[group action|acts]] as an [[automorphism group]] of the design. It is [[Group action#Transitivity properties|sharply transitive]] on both points and blocks.<ref>{{harvnb|van Lint|Wilson|1992|loc=p. 331 - Theorem 27.2}}. The theorem only states point transitivity, but block transitivity follows from this by the second corollary on p. 330.</ref> 
** In particular, if <math>\lambda=1</math>, then the difference set gives rise to a [[projective plane]]. An example of a (7,3,1) difference set in the group <math>\mathbb{Z}/7\mathbb{Z}</math> is the subset <math>\{1,2,4\}</math>. The translates of this difference set form the [[Fano plane]].
* Since every difference set gives a [[Block design#Symmetric BIBDs|symmetric design]], the parameter set must satisfy the [[Bruck–Ryser–Chowla theorem]].<ref>{{harvnb|Colbourn|Dinitz|2007|loc=p. 420  (18.7 Remark 2)}}</ref>
* Not every [[Block design#Symmetric BIBDs|symmetric design]] gives a difference set.<ref>{{harvnb|Colbourn|Dinitz|2007|loc=p. 420 (18.7 Remark 1)}}</ref>

==Equivalent and isomorphic difference sets==
Two difference sets <math>D_1</math> in group <math>G_1</math> and <math>D_2</math> in group <math>G_2</math> are '''equivalent''' if there is a [[group isomorphism]] <math>\psi</math> between <math>G_1</math> and <math>G_2</math> such that <math>D_1^{\psi} = \{d^{\psi}\colon d \in D_1 \} = g D_2</math> for some <math>g \in G_2.</math> The two difference sets are '''isomorphic''' if the designs <math>dev(D_1)</math> and <math>dev(D_2)</math> are isomorphic as block designs.

Equivalent difference sets are isomorphic, but there exist examples of isomorphic difference sets which are not equivalent.  In the cyclic difference set case, all known isomorphic difference sets are equivalent.<ref>{{harvnb|Colbourn|Dinitz|2007|loc=p. 420 (Remark 18.9)}}</ref>

==Multipliers==
A '''multiplier''' of a difference set <math>D</math> in group <math>G</math> is a [[group automorphism]] <math>\phi</math> of <math>G</math> such that <math>D^{\phi} = gD</math> for some <math>g \in G.</math> If <math>G</math> is abelian and <math>\phi</math> is the automorphism that maps <math>h \mapsto h^t</math>, then <math>t</math> is called a ''numerical'' or ''Hall'' '''multiplier'''.<ref>{{harvnb|van Lint|Wilson|1992|loc=p. 345}}</ref>

The '''multiplier conjecture''' predicts, in particular, that if ''p'' is a [[prime number|prime]] dividing <math>k-\lambda</math> and not dividing ''v'', then the automorphism <math>g\mapsto g^p</math> is a multiplier. This is known when <math>p>\lambda</math> and <math>G</math> is abelian, a result called the First Multiplier Theorem. A more general result, the Second Multiplier Theorem, says that if <math>D</math> is a <math>(v,k,\lambda)</math>-difference set in an abelian group <math>G</math> of exponent <math>v^*</math> (the [[least common multiple]] of the [[order (group theory)|orders]] of its elements), and <math>t</math> is an [[integer]] [[coprime]] to <math>v</math>, then the following condition is sufficient for <math>t</math> to be a numerical multiplier: there is a divisor <math>m</math> of <math>k-\lambda</math> with <math>\gcd(m,v)=1</math> and <math>m>\lambda</math> such that, for every prime ''p'' dividing ''m'', there is an integer ''i'' with <math>t\equiv p^i\pmod{v^*}</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|van Lint|Wilson|1992|loc=p. 349 (Theorem 28.7)}}</ref> Later work showed that the assumption <math>m>\lambda</math> can be replaced by a weaker divisibility condition, but the full multiplier conjecture remains open.<ref name="LeungMaSchmidt2014">{{cite journal |last1=Leung |first1=Ka Hin |last2=Ma |first2=Siu Lun |last3=Schmidt |first3=Bernhard |title=A multiplier theorem |journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A |volume=124 |pages=228–243 |year=2014 |doi=10.1016/j.jcta.2014.02.001}}</ref><ref name="GordonSchmidt2016">{{cite journal |last1=Gordon |first1=Daniel M. |last2=Schmidt |first2=Bernhard |title=A survey of the multiplier conjecture |journal=Designs, Codes and Cryptography |volume=78 |issue=1 |pages=221–236 |year=2016 |doi=10.1007/s10623-015-0153-8}}</ref>

For example, 2 is a multiplier of the (7,3,1)-difference set mentioned above.

It has been mentioned that a numerical multiplier of a difference set <math>D</math> in an abelian group <math>G</math> fixes a translate of <math>D</math>, but it can also be shown that there is a translate of <math>D</math> which is fixed by all numerical multipliers of <math>D.</math><ref>{{harvnb|Beth|Jungnickel|Lenz|1986|loc=p. 280 (Theorem 4.6)}}</ref>

==Ryser and Lander conjectures==
{{unsolved|mathematics|If an abelian group of order <math>v</math> contains a difference set of order <math>n</math>, and a prime <math>p</math> divides both <math>v</math> and <math>n</math>, must the Sylow <math>p</math>-subgroup of the group be non-cyclic?}}
In terms of the order <math>n=k-\lambda</math>, Ryser's cyclic difference-set conjecture states that a difference set in a [[cyclic group]] must satisfy <math>\gcd(v,n)=1</math>. For a Menon–Hadamard difference set with parameters <math>(4u^2,2u^2-u,u^2-u)</math>, the order is <math>u^2</math>; consequently, the [[Ryser's conjecture on circulant Hadamard matrices|circulant Hadamard conjecture]] is a special case.<ref name="LeungMaSchmidt2004">{{cite journal |last1=Leung |first1=Ka Hin |last2=Ma |first2=Siu Lun |last3=Schmidt |first3=Bernhard |title=Nonexistence of abelian difference sets: Lander's conjecture for prime power orders |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=356 |issue=11 |pages=4343–4358 |year=2004 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-03-03365-8}}</ref>

'''Lander's conjecture''', proposed by [[Eric S. Lander]] in 1983, strengthens Ryser's conjecture. It states that if an abelian group <math>G</math> of order <math>v</math> contains a difference set of order <math>n</math>, and a prime <math>p</math> divides both <math>v</math> and <math>n</math>, then the [[Sylow theorems|Sylow]] <math>p</math>-subgroup of <math>G</math> is not cyclic.<ref name="Lander1983">{{cite book |last=Lander |first=Eric S. |title=Symmetric Designs: An Algebraic Approach |series=London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series |volume=74 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1983 |page=224 |isbn=978-0-521-28693-0 |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511662164}}</ref> Since every Sylow subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic, Lander's conjecture implies Ryser's cyclic difference-set conjecture.

Lander's conjecture is unresolved in general. It has been proved when the order of the difference set is a power of a prime greater than 3, and for all difference sets in the McFarland, Spence, and Davis–Jedwab–Chen families.<ref name="LeungSchmidt2005">{{cite journal |last1=Leung |first1=Ka Hin |last2=Schmidt |first2=Bernhard |title=The field descent method |journal=Designs, Codes and Cryptography |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=171–188 |year=2005 |doi=10.1007/s10623-004-1703-7}}</ref> If the order is a power of 2 or 3 and the relevant Sylow subgroup is cyclic, then that subgroup must have order 2 or 3, respectively, and the parameters are restricted to a small number of exceptional forms.<ref name="LeungMaSchmidt2010">{{cite journal |last1=Leung |first1=Ka Hin |last2=Ma |first2=Siu Lun |last3=Schmidt |first3=Bernhard |title=On Lander's conjecture for difference sets whose order is a power of 2 or 3 |journal=Designs, Codes and Cryptography |volume=56 |issue=1 |pages=79–84 |year=2010 |doi=10.1007/s10623-009-9344-5}}</ref> The conjecture is also known for all Hadamard difference sets of order at most 529.<ref name="FengLeungSchmidtSmith2014">{{cite journal |last1=Feng |first1=Tao |last2=Leung |first2=Ka Hin |last3=Schmidt |first3=Bernhard |last4=Smith |first4=Ken W. |title=Hadamard difference sets related to Lander's conjecture |journal=Journal of Algebra |volume=403 |pages=29–47 |year=2014 |doi=10.1016/j.jalgebra.2013.11.027}}</ref>

Explicit small open cases are known. Baumert and Gordon settled the existence of cyclic <math>(v,k,\lambda)</math>-difference sets for all <math>k\le 150</math> except two parameter sets, and tabulated the undecided cases with <math>150<k\le 300</math>. The smallest undecided cyclic parameter set with <math>\gcd(v,n)>1</math> is <math>(465,145,45)</math>, of order <math>n=100</math>; here 5 divides both <math>v</math> and <math>n</math>, so Ryser's conjecture, and hence Lander's, predicts that no such difference set exists.<ref name="BaumertGordon2004">{{cite book |last1=Baumert |first1=Leonard D. |last2=Gordon |first2=Daniel M. |chapter=On the existence of cyclic difference sets with small parameters |editor1-last=van der Poorten |editor1-first=Alf |editor2-last=Stein |editor2-first=Andreas |title=High Primes and Misdemeanours: Lectures in Honour of the 60th Birthday of Hugh Cowie Williams |series=Fields Institute Communications |volume=41 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |year=2004 |pages=61–68 |arxiv=math/0304502}}</ref>

==Parameters==
Some important infinite parameter families, considered up to complementation, are:<ref>{{harvnb|Colbourn|Dinitz|2007|loc=pp. 422-425}}</ref>

*<math>((q^{n+2}-1)/(q-1), (q^{n+1}-1)/(q-1), (q^n-1)/(q-1))</math>-difference set for some [[prime power]] <math>q</math> and some positive integer <math>n</math>. These are known as the ''classical parameters'' and there are many constructions of difference sets having these parameters.
*<math>(4n-1,2n-1,n-1)</math>-difference set for some positive integer {{nowrap|<math>n</math>.}} Difference sets with {{nowrap|1=''v'' = 4''n'' − 1}} are called ''Paley-type difference sets''.
*<math>(4n^2,2n^2-n,n^2-n)</math>-difference set for some positive integer {{nowrap|<math>n</math>.}} A difference set with these parameters is called a ''Hadamard difference set'' or ''Menon difference set''. The existence of such a difference set in a ''cyclic'' group is the subject of [[Ryser's conjecture on circulant Hadamard matrices]], a well-known open problem.
*<math>(q^{n+1}(1+(q^{n+1}-1)/(q-1)),q^n(q^{n+1}-1)/(q-1),q^n(q^n-1)/(q-1))</math>-difference set for some prime power <math>q</math> and some positive integer {{nowrap|<math>n</math>.}} Known as the ''McFarland parameters''.
*<math>(3^{n+1}(3^{n+1}-1)/2,3^n(3^{n+1}+1)/2,3^n(3^n+1)/2)</math>-difference set for some positive integer {{nowrap|<math>n</math>.}} Known as the ''Spence parameters''.
*<math>(4q^{2n}(q^{2n}-1)/(q-1),q^{2n-1}(1+2(q^{2n}-1)/(q+1)),q^{2n-1}(q^{2n-1}+1)(q-1)/(q+1))</math>-difference set for some prime power <math>q</math> and some positive integer {{nowrap|<math>n</math>.}} Difference sets with these parameters are called ''Davis–Jedwab–Chen difference sets''.

==Selected constructions==
In many constructions of difference sets, the groups that are used are related to the additive and multiplicative groups of [[finite field]]s. The notation used to denote these fields differs according to discipline. In this section, <math>{\rm GF}(q)</math> is the [[Galois field]] of order <math>q,</math> where <math>q</math> is a prime power. The group under addition is denoted by <math>G = ({\rm GF}(q), +)</math>, while <math>{\rm GF}(q)^*</math> is the multiplicative group of non-zero elements.

* Paley <math>(4n-1, 2n-1, n-1)</math>-difference set:
::Let <math>q = 4n -1</math> be a prime power. In the group <math>G = ({\rm GF}(q), +)</math>, let <math>D</math> be the set of all non-zero squares.

* Singer <math>((q^{n+2}-1)/(q-1), (q^{n+1}-1)/(q-1), (q^n-1)/(q-1))</math>-difference set: 
::Let <math>G={\rm GF}(q^{n+2})^*/{\rm GF}(q)^*</math>. Then the set <math>D=\{x\in G~|~{\rm Tr}_{q^{n+2}/q}(x)=0\}</math> is a <math>((q^{n+2}-1)/(q-1), (q^{n+1}-1)/(q-1), (q^n-1)/(q-1))</math>-difference set, where <math>{\rm Tr}_{q^{n+2}/q}:{\rm GF}(q^{n+2})\rightarrow{\rm GF}(q)</math> is the [[trace function]] <math>\rm{Tr}_{q^{n+2}/q}(x) = x+x^q+\cdots+x^{q^{n+1}}.</math>

* [[Twin prime]] power <math> \left ( q^2 + 2q, \frac{q^2 + 2q -1}{2}, \frac{q^2+2q-3}{4} \right )</math>-difference set when <math>q</math> and <math>q+2</math> are both prime powers:
::In the group <math>G = ({\rm GF}(q), +) \oplus ({\rm GF}(q+2), +)</math>, let <math>D = \{(x,y) \colon y = 0 \text{ or } x \text{ and } y \text{ are non-zero and both are squares or both are non-squares} \}.</math><ref>{{harvnb|Colbourn|Dinitz|2007|loc=p. 425 (Construction 18.49)}}</ref>

==History==
The systematic use of cyclic difference sets and methods for the construction of symmetric block designs dates back to [[R. C. Bose]] and a seminal paper of his in 1939.<ref>{{citation|first=R.C.|last=Bose|title=On the construction of balanced incomplete block designs|journal=Annals of Eugenics|volume=9|year=1939|issue=4 |pages=353&ndash;399|doi=10.1111/j.1469-1809.1939.tb02219.x|jfm=65.1110.04|zbl=0023.00102|doi-access=free}}</ref> However, various examples appeared earlier than this, such as the "Paley Difference Sets" which date back to 1933.<ref>{{harvnb|Wallis|1988|loc=p. 69}}</ref> The generalization of the cyclic difference set concept to more general groups is due to [[Richard Bruck|R.H. Bruck]]<ref>{{citation|first=R.H.|last=Bruck| authorlink=Richard Bruck | title=Difference sets in a finite group|journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society|volume=78|year=1955|issue=2 |pages=464&ndash;481|doi=10.2307/1993074 |jstor=1993074 | zbl=0065.13302 |doi-access=free}}</ref> in 1955.<ref>{{harvnb|van Lint|Wilson|1992|loc=p. 340}}</ref> Multipliers were introduced by [[Marshall Hall (mathematician)|Marshall Hall Jr.]]<ref>{{citation|last=Hall Jr.|first=Marshall|authorlink=Marshall Hall (mathematician) | title=Cyclic projective planes|journal= Duke Mathematical Journal|volume=14|year=1947|issue=4 |pages=1079&ndash;1090|doi=10.1215/s0012-7094-47-01482-8 | zbl=0029.22502|s2cid=119846649 }}</ref> in 1947.<ref>{{harvnb|Beth|Jungnickel|Lenz|1986|loc=p. 275}}</ref>

==Application==

Xia, Zhou and [[Georgios B. Giannakis|Giannakis]] used difference sets to construct complex vector [[codebook]]s that attain the [[Welch bounds|Welch lower bound]] on maximum cross-correlation amplitude in certain cases.

==Generalisations==
A <math>(v,k,\lambda,s)</math> '''difference family''' is a set of subsets <math>B=\{B_1,\ldots,B_s\}</math> of a group <math>G</math> such that the order of <math>G</math> is <math>v</math>, the size of <math>B_i</math> is <math>k</math> for all <math>i</math>, and every non-identity element of <math>G</math> can be expressed as a product <math>d_1d_2^{-1}</math> of elements of <math>B_i</math> for some <math>i</math> (i.e. both <math>d_1,d_2</math> come from the same <math>B_i</math>) in exactly <math>\lambda</math> ways.

A difference set is a difference family with <math>s=1.</math> The parameter equation above generalises to <math>s(k^2-k)=(v-1)\lambda.</math><ref>{{harvnb|Beth|Jungnickel|Lenz|1986|loc=p. 310 (2.8.a)}}</ref> 
The development <math>dev (B) = \{B_i+g: i=1,\ldots,s, g \in G\}</math> of a difference family is a [[Block design|2-design]].
Every 2-design with a regular automorphism group is <math>dev (B)</math> for some difference family <math>B.</math>
